_comment: Sites neither Wikidata query returns — either because they carry no heritage designation there, or because they sit outside the 25 km sweep. Every coordinate names its source; none were estimated. Descriptions are written here from facts stated in the cited sources, not copied from them.
name: Chinese Temple, Achipur
coord_source: Wikidata Q137780795; the OpenStreetMap node for the same temple agrees to within ~100 m
description: Yang Tai Chow — known in Calcutta as Tong Achew — arrived in 1778 and was granted 650 bighas on the Hooghly by Warren Hastings, at forty-five rupees a year, for a sugar plantation and mill. The Chinese workers he brought over made this the first Chinese settlement in India. He died within a few years and his community moved upriver to Tiretta Bazar, leaving this temple, among the oldest surviving Chinese religious sites in the country, with Achew's horseshoe-shaped grave a short walk away. Kolkata's Chinese families still come down for the New Year.

name: Sea Ip Church
description: A Cantonese clan temple up a narrow stair off Chattawala Gully, and the grandest of the Tiretta Bazar six. The association dates from 1882 and the present building from 1905. On the Kolkata Municipal Corporation's graded list as a Chinese temple.

name: Toong On Church
description: Cantonese migrants from Koon Tong bought the plot on Blackburn Lane in 1917 and finished the temple in 1924. The ground floor became the Nanking Restaurant in 1925 — Calcutta's, and probably India's, first Chinese restaurant. It declined after the 1962 war and closed in the late 1970s; the temple above it survived.

name: Gee Hing Church
description: One of the six clan temples that survive in Tiretta Bazar, Calcutta's original Chinatown, and on the Kolkata Municipal Corporation's graded list as a Chinese temple. The Gee Hing association also keeps a burial ground of its own off Meher Ali Lane.

name: Nam Soon Church
description: A clan temple on Damzen Lane, on the graded list as a Chinese temple. The Nam Soon association, like the others in Tiretta Bazar, ran a temple, a school and a burial ground for its members; its cemetery is on Mathur Babu Lane.

name: Sea Voi Yune Leong Futh Church
coord_source: OpenStreetMap node, name "Sea Voi Chinese Temple"
description: A Chinese temple on Blackburn Lane, carried on the Kolkata Municipal Corporation's graded list under its full name, Sea Voi Yune Leong Futh Church. It stands within a hundred metres of four other clan temples, all raised by the community that moved up from Achipur after Tong Achew's death.

name: Chun Nee Thong Church
description: The sixth of the Tiretta Bazar Chinese temples. Romanisations of these names vary a great deal between the graded list, the street and the map: the register and local accounts also record a Choong Ye Thong Church a few doors away on New Meredith Street, rebuilt in three storeys around 1932, which may well be this same building under another spelling.

name: Gillander House
description: Built for Gillanders, Arbuthnot & Co., one of the Scottish managing agencies that ran Clive Street, and completed in 1909. It resists the labels the rest of the city accepts — the Writers' Building is Greco-Roman, the High Court Gothic, Esplanade Mansions Art Nouveau — partly because its architect, Harry Stuart Goodhart-Rendel, was a composer as much as a designer.

name: Royal Insurance Building
description: Royal Insurance was founded in Liverpool in 1845; its Calcutta office went up on Dalhousie Square sixty years later, in 1905. One of the mercantile palaces that make the square a commercial rather than a governmental set piece.

name: Hong Kong House
description: The Calcutta premises of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, on the south side of Dalhousie Square. No construction date for it is on public record.

name: The Calcutta Collectorate
description: Built in 1892, ten years after the Writers' Building, on the ground where the Old Fort William of 1696–1706 once stood — which makes this the site of the Black Hole. Curzon put up a replica of the Black Hole monument here in 1901; it too was eventually removed.

name: North Park Street Cemetery
description: The second of the Park Street burial grounds, opened in 1797 across the road from the South Park Street cemetery when that one filled. Very little of it is left; the Robertson monument is the piece people still go looking for.

name: Jewish Cemetery, Narkeldanga
description: The burial ground of Calcutta's Baghdadi Jewish community, out on Narkeldanga Main Road. Its prayer hall was finished in 1921. The community that filled it — the Ezras, the Gubbays, the Nahoums — has almost entirely gone, and the cemetery is now one of the fullest records left of it.

name: Nipponzan Myohoji Japanese Buddhist Temple
coord_source: OpenStreetMap node, name=Nipponzan Myohoji Buddhist Temple
description: A temple of the Japanese Nipponzan-Myōhōji order, built on Lake Road in 1935 — four years before the Second World War overtook the community that had raised it.

name: Myanmar (Burma) Buddhist Temple
description: A Burmese Buddhist temple off Eden Hospital Road, at the edge of the old Chinatown quarter — a survival of the Burmese community that came to Calcutta while Burma was governed from here.

name: Nizam Palace
coord_source: OpenStreetMap way at 234/4 A. J. C. Bose Road, the Nizam Palace complex
description: Built by J. C. Galstaun, the Armenian horse-breeder turned property magnate who put up a good deal of south-central Calcutta, and later sold to the Nizam of Hyderabad, whose title stuck to it. It is now a central government office complex.

name: Temple Chambers
address: 6, Old Post Office St, B.B.D. Bagh
description: Vincent Esch's office block on the corner of Esplanade Row West and Old Post Office Street, built in 1910 and let out as chambers to the solicitors and agents who worked the courts opposite.

name: Wallace House
address: 4, Bankshall St, Fairley Place, B.B.D. Bagh
description: The Calcutta house of Shaw Wallace, the firm Robert Gordon Shaw and Charles Wallace built from 1886 out of tea, jute, timber and later oil. It still stands at 4 Bankshall Street.

name: Graham Building
address: 14, Netaji Subhas Rd, Murgighata, B.B.D. Bagh
description: One of the mercantile blocks on Clive Street, built for Graham & Co., among the Scottish managing agencies that ran the jute and tea trades from this quarter mile.

name: Ralli Brothers
coord_source: located to the street, not the building footprint
description: The Calcutta office of Ralli Brothers, the Greek trading house founded by five brothers from Chios that became one of the largest exporters of jute and grain out of Bengal.

name: Mackinnon Mackenzie & Co.
address: 16, Strand Rd, Fairley Place, B.B.D. Bagh
description: The Strand Road offices of Mackinnon Mackenzie, founded in Cossipore in 1847 by two Campbeltown Scots and agents for the British India Steam Navigation Company, which at its height ran more ships than any line in the world.

name: House of Arathoon Stephen
description: The Camac Street house of Arathoon Stephen, the Armenian who arrived in Calcutta with nothing, made a fortune in property and built the Grand Hotel on Chowringhee.

name: Dumraon House
description: Built in 1922 as the Calcutta residence of the Maharaja of Dumraon, one of the Bihar houses that kept a town address here for the season.

name: Murshidabad House
description: The Park Street town house of the Nawabs of Murshidabad — the family the Company displaced at Plassey, keeping a residence in the city that replaced their capital.

name: The Metropolitan Nursing Home
description: The Metropolitan Laboratory and Nursing Home on Theatre Road, now Shakespeare Sarani — one of the private medical establishments that grew up around the European quarter.

name: Duff College (Jorabagan Police Station)
description: Alexander Duff's Free Church Institution opened here on 4 March 1844, teaching in English to Bengali students and feeding the founding of the University of Calcutta. The building is now Jorabagan police station.

name: Baneshwar Shiva Temple
description: A Shiva temple on Banamali Sarkar Street whose date nobody has been able to fix; the family house beside it went up between 1740 and 1750, so the temple is probably of the same generation.

name: Niyamatullah Ghat Masjid
description: A mosque on Nimtala Ghat Street, in the stretch of north Calcutta where the burning ghat, the Ahiritola boat crossing and the potters' quarter run into each other.

name: Zohra Begum Masjid
description: A mosque in Tollygunge, in the quarter settled by the family and retainers of Tipu Sultan after their exile to Bengal.

name: Ezra Mansion
description: One of the commercial blocks put up by the Ezras, the Baghdadi Jewish family whose name is on a street, a hospital and a good deal of central Calcutta's property.

name: Neveh Shalome Synagogue
description: The oldest synagogue foundation in Calcutta, on Brabourne Road, standing a few minutes' walk from both Beth El and the Maghen David — three synagogues for a community that has now almost entirely left.

name: Basu Bati
description: The Bagbazar house of the Basu brothers, still unfinished when Mahendra Nath Basu died in August 1874. It became a meeting place of the swadeshi years, and its terracotta front is among the finest in north Calcutta.

name: Radhanath Temple (Bawali Mondal)
address: Radhakanta temple of Ramnath Mondal, Chetla
description: Begun in 1796 and finished in 1807 by the Mondal family of Bawali, on the lane in Chetla that still carries their name.

name: Goenka Ghat
description: The Ramchandra Goenka zenana bathing ghat, erected in 1916 — a screened ghat for women, next to the chhatri and well the Goenka family had built on the same stretch of the Strand in 1888.

name: Royal Exchange
address: The Bengal Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Royal Exchange
description: Completed and opened in 1918 by Lord Ronaldshay at a cost of five lakh rupees, and still lettered ROYAL EXCHANGE across its front although the street outside was renamed India Exchange Place. It houses the Bengal Chamber of Commerce.

name: McLeod House
description: The Calcutta house of McLeod & Co., founded in 1887 and one of the largest of the Scottish managing agencies, running collieries, jute mills and the light railways of Bengal.

name: Turner Morrison & Co.
coord_source: located to the street, not the building footprint
description: The Lyons Range offices of Turner Morrison, established in Calcutta in 1864 and within thirteen years the third largest shipping agency in the port.

name: New Central Telegraph Office
coord_source: located to the street, not the building footprint
description: The Central Telegraph Office off Dalhousie Square. The older building behind it was designed in 1868 and finished in 1876, when a telegram from here reached London in minutes and a letter took six weeks.

name: Court of Small Causes
description: The Calcutta Court of Small Causes on Bankshall Street, descended from the small cause courts chartered for the three presidency towns by George II in 1753 to settle petty civil suits quickly and cheaply.

name: Baro Ras Bari, Chetla
description: The larger of the two Ras Baris on Tollygunge Road, built around 1828 with the rows of aat-chala Shiva temples that flank the courtyard.

name: Chhoto Ras Bari, Chetla
description: The smaller Ras Bari, begun in March 1846 and finished on the last day of Chaitra 1253 — 2 April 1847 — a date its own inscription records in the Bengali calendar.

name: Bengali War Memorial
description: The memorial in College Square to the Bengali soldiers of the First World War — raised against the standing claim that Bengalis would not fight.

name: Treasury Building
description: Built between 1882 and 1884 on Government Place West, opposite the Town Hall, to hold the government's cash and its accounts.

name: Old Telegraph Office (Dead Letter Office)
address: Dead Letter Building, 33 B.B.D. Bag South
description: Built between 1873 and 1876 with a bell tower over eighty feet high, and later given over to the Dead Letter Office — the department that opened undeliverable post to find out where it should have gone.

name: Martin & Co.
coord_source: located to the street, not the building footprint
description: The Mission Row offices of Martin & Co., the firm of Sir Rajendra Nath Mookerjee, which finished the Victoria Memorial, built the Belur Math and the Ochterlony Monument, and laid much of the city's steel and concrete.

name: Standard Life Assurance Building
address: Standard Life Assurance Building, B.B.D. Bagh
description: Built in 1896 to the designs of Frederick William Stevens, the architect of Bombay's Victoria Terminus, for the Standard Life Assurance Company of Edinburgh.
